title: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues
description: The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition.The London insti
body: The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition.The London institution has announced changes to how visitors see the historic work over concerns of overcrowding."Anyone that doesn't have a good experience, we're really sorry about that and we want to put it right," Nicholas Cullinan told the BBC's culture and media editor Katie Razzall.The new plans include longer opening hours, an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.Some people reported waits of up to two hours. Last week, hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early for a private event."You don't want anyone that comes to see it to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons," Cullinan said."Obviously we want everyone that comes to have a fantastic experience. To put it into context, we're three weeks into the exhibition run. Next week, we'll hit our 100,000th visitor, which is a pretty extraordinary statistic. The vast number of visitors report having a very good experience."Asked if the museum team had asked the embroidery's home museum in Bayeux for advice on queue management and timings, Cullinan said they had. He also denied the museum had let too many people book tickets and said that the issues arose because visitors want to spend more time with the work than expected.The problem "isn't just the interest, it's that people want to spend more time than anticipated. And that's a good thing. We want people to come and enjoy it, but it means we have to adjust accordingly and that's what we're doing," Cullinan said.Some visitors have been spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry, meaning others have to move through more quickly, he said.While the museum is reimbursing those who have been turned away, when asked if they might also compensate people for travel costs, Cullinan said it was "a possibility", but added that  "obviously this is an incredibly expensive exhibition to mount."The exhibition has also faced some criticism over accessibility, but Cullinan said they had done "everything they could", given the stipulation that the tapestry had to be laid flat, making it more difficult for wheelchair users to see.Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day.Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when additional tickets go on sale in October and January.Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared to the €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free.The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

schema.headline: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues

title: Jeremy Clarkson makes surprise appearance at Tory conference
description: Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conferen
body: Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food."It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now. "But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather."Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers.Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

schema.headline: Jeremy Clarkson makes surprise appearance at Tory conference

title: Donald Trump says a 'threat' led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford
description: US President Donald Trump has said the United States moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.The Pentagon confirme
body: US President Donald Trump has said the United States moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US knew of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised "our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat had led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase."And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy," he told a gaggle of reporters outside the White House in Washington.He added that Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but did not confirm who.RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.Speaking earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident.US Vice President JD Vance later said the bombers were moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington feels Iran is doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

schema.headline: Donald Trump says a 'threat' led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford

title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and riot police
description: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as stude
body: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch."The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days. There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.The AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade."He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified."Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school. "At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media. "Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on."In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began.Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered"."His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying."It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country.High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands.More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according to AFP, with around 85% of them minors.The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected.Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted.But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets.Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest.In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced.Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October.

schema.headline: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and riot police

title: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
description: It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.Yet that
body: It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country.The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism.The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally.What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed.Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion.The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin.So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy.Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership.And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership.In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy. The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections. It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy.Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham.In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term.While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard".Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc.And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum."Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda.

schema.headline: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote

title: Ho Chi Minh city: Twelve arrested for allegedly running cat trafficking ring in Vietnam
description: Twelve men have been arrested in Vietnam after allegedly confessing to stealing and selling around 2,700 cats, Ho Chi Minh City police have said. Cat
body: Twelve men have been arrested in Vietnam after allegedly confessing to stealing and selling around 2,700 cats, Ho Chi Minh City police have said. Cat traps, fur removal machines and measuring scales were among the items seized during the investigation. The men are suspected of taking the pets to be slaughtered for food.Police allege the suspects roamed through residential areas in small groups on motorbikes at night to steal the cats.The men reportedly used pieces of fish as bait, placing traps outside houses where they knew cats were kept, state media reported. Thirteen of the rescued felines have since been returned to their owners. According to the animal protection organisation Humane World for Animals, an estimated five million dogs and one million cats are captured, stolen, trafficked and slaughtered for meat in Vietnam every year. The consumption of dog and cat meat is legal in the country, where many restaurants openly advertise it on their menu. But vendors require permits that show the origin of the animals.Each group allegedly stole an average of four to 10 cats per night, according to a police statement in Ho Chi Minh City police department's official newspaper. On 8 July, police said they seized 50 cats, two weighing scales, 55 cat traps, 14 bags, 13 mobile phones, seven motorbikes, two fur-removing machines and 6.7 million Vietnamese dong ($257; £195).The 12 suspects were then brought in for questioning, and police say they confessed to stealing around 2,700 cats. Of the 50 cats that were seized, 13 have been returned to their owners, while the remaining are being kept at the animal welfare centre HavePaws.

schema.headline: Ho Chi Minh city: Twelve arrested for allegedly running cat trafficking ring in Vietnam

title: King's funding for Andrew is not for legal action against police
description: Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so
body: Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle.But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking.It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.This allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor is not from the Sovereign Grant, which is the £138m in public funding for the monarchy. It is drawn from the King's private money, which includes his income from the Duchy of Lancaster, private estates and his own investments and inheritances.At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace is now distancing itself from the former Duke of York's legal pushback.Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court over the lawfulness of warrants used for searches of Sandringham and Royal Lodge - in what has been Andrew's first public response since his arrest earlier this year.Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court".It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.A court hearing on Thursday afternoon will be part of Mountbatten-Windsor's bid to quash the warrants.The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in Sandringham."Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.Vamos said disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search."The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said connections had been severed.After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation.

schema.headline: King's funding for Andrew is not for legal action against police

title: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall
description: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for the BBC's director of news. She is a well-regarded high flier who has impressed in her roles at Panorama, Newsnight a
body: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for the BBC's director of news. She is a well-regarded high flier who has impressed in her roles at Panorama, Newsnight and Channel 4 News. She is currently the BBC's director of news documentaries and long form journalism. But she hasn't been in that role for long and hasn't spent years leading huge teams of people (BBC News' global newsroom has around 4,500 staff).A lack of that kind of experience might have been problematic in the past. But the BBC's new director general comes from Google. Tech companies regularly appoint people who may not have the direct experience for a role but have the strategic vision and drive to make a difference. He is talking about distinctive journalism and reinvention.Jupp's appointment signals a direction of travel both on the change that the new boss thinks is required and also on the use of technology. BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of newsBefore Jupp took up her role in documentaries, she had moved to the US and was a senior member of the BBC's AI team, developing and leading the BBC's approach to artificial intelligence.It feels significant that the former Google boss has chosen someone with that experience to run his news teams, raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom.But the new director of news has a lot on her plate.She leads a news operation that is still reeling from a series of crises that eventually brought down her predecessor, Deborah Turness, as well as director general Tim Davie.She'll have to oversee the £51m in savings that news must make (one tenth of the £500m the entire BBC must find).Job cuts are already in train, journalists are having to reapply for their roles - and there is much more pain to come.Staff have told me they want clear direction and an end to the salami slicing of resources. They ask what are the priorities, what are the things we do that are crucial and which are less important?The teams she now leads will want a plan for how they can make such deep cuts without impacting the quality of what they do. BBC News stands or falls by its on-the-ground, eyewitness journalism. Some are asking how much of that can BBC News still afford to do.But there are also questions about whether the BBC needs to learn from its rivals by slimming down the number of stories it does and prioritizing the big hits. A streamlined BBC News.Her challenges are both editorial and practical.Brittin has talked about the bigger prize of getting the news division's trusted journalism to much larger numbers of people around the world. She has to deliver that.She will also need to give BBC News greater editorial confidence after years of political attack and the errors of recent years.Staff working in news would argue it was the current affairs side of the operation that previously let the organisation down. A documentary about the children of Gaza narrated by the son of a Hamas official. A documentary about Israel's assault on Gazan medical staff commissioned and then dropped by the BBC and later shown on Channel 4.Then, of course, there are the revelations that a Panorama broadcast ahead of Donald Trump's reelection as President had spliced together two clips of the President's speech on the day of the riots on Capitol Hill - changing the editorial meaning. BBC chair Samir Shah apologised to Trump who is suing the BBC for $10bn. The court proceedings are still playing out.Perhaps promoting Jupp - who took over the BBC News' current affairs department after the scandals - to the top of News is a signal she will grip what some have viewed as a weak spot with rigour.Trust is one of the BBC's core values. It's listed on the back of our work passes as "the foundation of the BBC". The new boss will need to make sure that the BBC remains the place of record. An organisation that is trusted.It's still the most trusted source of news, but there are growing numbers of people on all sides of the political spectrum who don't feel the BBC speaks for them.Many will argue that is because people live in echo chambers online, and don't want to hear other voices.But any loss of trust is corrosive.

schema.headline: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall

title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia, Rubio says
description: The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.Secretary of State Marco Rub
body: The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was concern the incident could have led to the spread of pneumonic plague, but that there was no cause for alarm.  Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said that "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".Unconfirmed reports had suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague is found naturally among wild rodents.No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since her death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature. "If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.  It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.     "Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.    He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here.""People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said. "It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible."Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.

schema.headline: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia, Rubio says

title: China Open: Daniil Medvedev disqualified from Novak Djokovic match after hitting spectator with ball
description: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from the China Open after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball during his semi-final against Novak Djokovic.Th
body: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from the China Open after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball during his semi-final against Novak Djokovic.Third seed Medvedev trailed Djokovic 7-5 5-3 when the Serb hit a winner beyond him for 15-15.The ball ricocheted off the back of the court and Medvedev swiped at a backhand in annoyance, sending the ball into the air and hitting a spectator who was sitting in the front row of the stand behind him.The fan doubled over holding his face and was still holding his eye as he was helped out of the arena.After speaking with umpire Mohamed Lahyani and an ATP official, Russia's Medvedev approached the net to shake hands with Djokovic."Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all," Medvedev said."I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels."I just hope he's OK. That's the most important. I just really care about him right now."Djokovic - who was defaulted from the 2020 US Open for a similar incident - expressed sympathy for the fan and Medvedev afterwards."It's a bit of a shock to be honest. I hope that person is not badly injured," he said."I also feel sorry for Daniil. I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match."I am sure that Daniil did not want to do this intentionally."Defaults in tennis are rare and only occur when players violate the sport's code of conduct.Violations include ball abuse, physical or verbal abuse, or racquet abuse. Players can receive three code violations and then be disqualified if they receive another, but Medvedev's offence was serious enough to instantly default him.He will now lose the points and prize money he had earned in Beijing - a run that would have seen him return to inside the world's top five.The 30-year-old is a combustible character who has struggled to control his emotions throughout his career.He had a meltdown at last year's US Open when a photographer walked on court, and was fined almost £31,500 ($42,500) for his behaviour.In April, he obliterated a racquet after losing 6-0 6-0 at the Monte Carlo Masters and was again fined for unsportsmanlike conduct.Medvedev told BBC Sport in 2025 that he was attempting to work on his on-court behaviour."When I'm on the court I hate to lose; I love to win. My first goal is to win the match, so it brings a lot of adrenaline out and it brings all the energy out," he said."Sometimes it is a good energy. Sometimes it is a bad one."

title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario AmodeiByKali HaysTechnology reporter
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario AmodeiByKali HaysTechnology reporter in San Francisco and Daniel BushWashington correspondentThe US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday.Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay.Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence departmentThe Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system."The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said."Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. Image source, EPAImage caption, Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White HouseThe BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.Figure caption, 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AISources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage. The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration. Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week. After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI."How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

title: ECB will 'look at' funding West Indies Test if required, says Richard Thompson
description: The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) would "look at" the unusual step of funding a women's Test in the West Indies next year in order to aid Engl
body: The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) would "look at" the unusual step of funding a women's Test in the West Indies next year in order to aid England's Ashes preparations.The Test in the Caribbean, part of a multi-format series in the spring of 2027, was announced in 2024 and is scheduled before England's bid to regain the Ashes from Australia.Last week, Cricket West Indies (CWI) announced a wide range of money-saving measures, including cuts to player contracts.In March, a women's Test that West Indies were due to host against Australia was cancelled, though the white-ball element of that tour went ahead.There have been no discussions between the ECB and CWI about cancelling the Test.The tour as a whole – including three T20s and three one-day internationals in April and May of next year – is not under threat, though exact dates and venues are still to be confirmed.Asked by BBC Sport if the Test was in doubt, ECB chair Richard Thompson said: "I hope not. That's not expected to be cancelled. I hope it will take place."However, when it was put to Thompson that the ECB may need to provide some funding for the Test to take place, he said his organisation would "look at" the situation should it arise.Governing bodies usually have reciprocal arrangements for the home board to pick up the logistical expenses of the visiting team, including things like travel and accommodation.In the West Indies, these can be inflated by the cost of flying West Indies and visiting players between islands. Last week, CWI said it has spent more than $80m on domestic air travel in the past 15 years.Thompson pointed to a similarly unusual situation when the Zimbabwe men's team played a Test in England last year, with the ECB paying the visitors a touring fee."We want that Test match to play out," said Thompson. "It's very important for us because our first women's match in the Ashes is the Headingley Test, so we need a good red-ball warm-up."We've got to be playing somewhere and we'd much prefer that to be the West Indies."We all have a huge sympathy for the West Indies, we all want to see a successful West Indian nation. They have very unique challenges and I hope through the International Cricket Council and others we can find a way through this."The first match of the multi-format women's Ashes series is the sole Test at Headingley in June – the only Test, men's or women's, staged north of Nottingham next summer.England have played one Test since they lost every game on the Ashes tour of Australia in early 2025 – a defeat by India at Lord's earlier this year.They have not played West Indies in a women's Test since 1979, while West Indies have not played a Test against anyone since a trip to Pakistan in 2004.The Test in West Indies is one part of England's Ashes Test preparations. In January, the squad will take part in a 10-day red-ball training camp in India.In 2023, England played Australia A and Australia played England A as Test warm-up matches and that arrangement could be replicated in 2027. Plans for domestic players to potentially be involved in some red-ball cricket in the early part of next season are also being finalised.Thompson was speaking at Lord's as the ECB launched initiatives to take cricket to more than 1,700 state secondary schools and more than 3,500 teachers.'Cricket for Teachers' and 'Secondary Countdown Cricket' are part of the ECB's aim to reach half of all state secondary schools in England and Wales by the end of 2028.Earlier this year, a report by the Sutton Trust found cricket to be one of the most elitist jobs in the country, with 59% of male professionals and 50% of women privately educated."We really want teachers to upskill and be able to coach," said Thompson. "The second part is to be able to do something no other team sport can do, which is bring boys and girls together until the age of 16."This adds to the pathway. It's another stepping stone for a late developer, or an opportunity for someone to think they want to play the game properly, with a hardball."It's meaningful in that we want to reach one and a half million children who have never played the game before. That's a significant programme and the ambition that sits behind this."

schema.headline: ECB will 'look at' funding West Indies Test if required, says Richard Thompson

title: Dawood Safi detained for killing Wayne Broadhurst in Uxbridge
description: Man who killed dog walker should be deported, says judgeImage source, Met PoliceImage caption, Dawood Safi was given an indefinite hospital order Upda
body: Man who killed dog walker should be deported, says judgeImage source, Met PoliceImage caption, Dawood Safi was given an indefinite hospital order Updated 3 hours agoAn Afghan refugee who killed a dog walker and attacked two other people in a "frenzy of violence" has been given an indefinite hospital order and recommended for deportation.Dawood Safi, 28, stabbed Wayne Broadhurst, 49, in the street during a series of knife attacks which began at Safi's home in Uxbridge, west London, on 27 October 2025, Southwark Crown Court heard. Safi, who was having paranoid delusions and hearing voices, attacked his landlord Shahzad Farrukh minutes before killing Broadhurst, and also stabbed a 14-year-old boy. The 28-year-old admitted manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.Mrs Justice Cutts, who told the court that Safi had been "in a psychotic state", said the final decision on whether he should be deported rested with the home secretary.Image source, Met PoliceImage caption, Wayne Broadhurst was walking his dog Harry when he was attackedA Home Office spokesperson said the attack was "horrific" and "appalling".They added: "The court has ordered the offender be detained indefinitely in a secure hospital. "Foreign nationals who commit serious crimes should expect to face the full force of the law, and we will always seek to remove those who pose a danger to the public where it is legally possible to do so."Decisions on deportation are considered carefully on a case-by-case basis in line with the law, and it would not be appropriate to comment further on an individual case."Image source, Broadhurst familyImage caption, The street cleaner was described as "a gentle and quiet man"In her sentencing remarks, the judge acknowledged the "devastating" impact of the crime on Broadhurst's family, and added that he was "a hard-working and decent man who was deeply loved".Cutts told Safi: "Wayne Broadhurst, a gentle and quiet man, had the misfortune to be walking his dog at the time. "As he emerged from the alleyway on to the street, you set upon and killed him in a frenzied, random, and completely unprovoked assault involving stabbing him at least 14 times."Broadhurst's partner, Ann Newman, told the court she had had a "future stolen from me" and described facing up to a daily battle with grief and loss.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Mrs Justice Cutts recommended Safi be deported, but said the final decision rested with the home secretarySafi, who appeared for his sentencing hearing on a video link from the high-security Broadmoor hospital, was born in the Kapisa province of northern Afghanistan.He was smuggled into the UK on the back of a lorry in November 2020 and lied about his age - saying he was 17 instead of 22 - to stand a better chance of asylum.He worked as an Uber driver, studied for a mechanics qualification at Uxbridge College and had no convictions since entering the country.He had sought help from doctors for his deteriorating mental health prior to the stabbings, which began at his home in Midhurst Gardens.'Paranoid beliefs'The court was told that in the three days before the stabbings, Safi had attended an appointment at his GP, had a mental health assessment at Hillingdon Hospital and had sought help at Hayes police station.After the stabbings, doctors concluded Safi was suffering from psychotic depression which had led to the violent offences.Dr Elliott Carthy, who assessed Safi at Broadmoor, said he had "paranoid and persecutory beliefs", and voices in his head contributed to his actions that day.He said a hospital order with restrictions was the best way to protect the public "going forward now and in anticipation of his release into the community".He said Safi was likely to spend at least five years at Broadmoor before being considered for transfer to a medium security facility where he would stay for several more years, and if he is released into the community he would be under strict conditions and subject to lifelong monitoring.Safi, who admitted manslaughter, was found guilty by a jury of attempting to murder Farrukh and pleaded guilty to causing actual bodily harm to the teenage boy, as well as possession of the knife.Prosecutors dropped a charge of murder after the guilty plea to manslaughter was entered, and after receiving expert reports on Safi's mental health.The judge told the court she would have sentenced Safi to life in prison with a minimum term of eight years if he had not been mentally unwell.

schema.headline: Dawood Safi detained for killing Wayne Broadhurst in Uxbridge

title: Man City charges scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
description: United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we
body: United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027.  United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

schema.headline: Man City charges scandal shines light on Man Utd finances

title: JJ Gabriel: No reconciliation in sight for rift with Manchester United
description: JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as
body: JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as new details of his efforts to leave Old Trafford emerge.The teenage forward - who turns 16 on Tuesday - features in the photographs that were released on Monday. It is understood the pictures were taken on 8 September - two days before he played his final game for the club and informed them of his intention to leave.It is virtually certain his next involvement in a United game will be as an opposition player.United still hold his registration and, according to sources close to Old Trafford, the club have made multiple attempts to reconcile the situation as part of their duty of care to the teenager. So far, it has been to no avail.Gabriel is now a target for several of Europe's top clubs, with Real Madrid and Barcelona among those taking a keen interest. He now has a European Union passport, which is thought could smooth his passage to the continent.However, while no clubs have approached United so far, they would consider legal action if any evidence of an illegal inducement by a club or agent - that would contravene regulations in relation to young players - was to emerge.While tensions between Gabriel's camp and United had been simmering for a number of months, sources have told BBC Sport the player's decision to seek a move away was ultimately triggered by his non-inclusion in Michael Carrick side for the Champions League encounter with Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September.The youngster's camp had expressed a desire for Gabriel to be used as a substitute against Sabah - which, on paper, was the easiest of United's league-phase games.Sources say the prospect of the Londoner coming on against Brighton in the EFL Cup on 16 September was also discussed, with United officials subsequently insistent that was the plan.Had he played in either match, Gabriel would have become United's youngest ever player.However, by the time the encounter with Fabian Hurzeler's side arrived, the striker had already told the club of his intention to quit and had left the country.Gabriel could not play against Sabah because he had not been registered on United's Uefa A list of players when it was announced on 3 September. The precise reasons for this have not been made clear.It did not prevent him scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game against them at Leigh Sports Village earlier on 10 September. While he has not been back to United since, it is not clear whether anything significant happened after that game.For their part, United believe they made it clear they view Gabriel as immensely important to their first-team future, even though sources have indicated the player did not report for the start of the academy's pre-season training schedule at the beginning of July - a week earlier than the senior squad - despite being asked to do so.Sources also say they lobbied the Premier League to allow the forward to use "JJ Gabriel" on the back of his shirt - which they believe underlined their commitment to the academy prospect.Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - but he is reported to have changed his name for commercial purposes.In addition, United say they have provided Gabriel with first-team care and services - included regular meetings with senior coaches and nutritionists.That he was included in the senior team photo is also viewed as further evidence of their commitment to his development and transition into first-team football.When Gabriel committed himself to United in the summer of 2025, the lure of breaking through at United, and the targets he could aim for, was strong.He was only 14 at the time but already he was looking towards the first team. Within a couple of months, Gabriel was called into senior training sessions by Ruben Amorim.Expectation grew to such an extent that interim boss Darren Fletcher was asked if it was possible the forward could make his competitive bow in the FA Cup third-round tie with Brighton in January.Fletcher - then Gabriel's coach at under-18 level - said no, believing the youngster wasn't physically ready.However, as he continued to excel at under-18 level, it seemed a case of when, not if, Gabriel would be given his chance.He ended the 2025-26 campaign as the Premier League's Under-18 player of the year and picked up the same award at United. It seemed certain he would be involved at the start of pre-season, when the majority of United's senior players would be absent after their World Cup exertions.What happened instead solidified existing doubts of those close to Gabriel that United were the right club for him.First, he was not part of Carrick's squad for the trip to Helsinki to face Wrexham in a friendly. On 24 July, he was an unused substitute against Rosenborg in Trondheim, a match in which Carrick made 10 outfield changes. Five of those players have since been sold or loaned out.Gabriel finally got his chance against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm on 1 August, when he replaced Bryan Mbeumo for the final eight minutes.That turned out to be it. He was on the bench for the final two games against Leeds and AC Milan, but did not get on. Against Leeds, former FA Youth Cup team-mate Dan Armer and 18-year-old newcomer Tynan Thompson were both introduced.

schema.headline: JJ Gabriel: No reconciliation in sight for rift with Manchester United
